items.stem: Who is credited with the discovery of the neutron?
items.markingKey: (c) The neutron was discovered by J. Chadwick (bombarding beryllium with alpha particles).

items.stem: The charge on a proton is:

Assertion (A): An atom is electrically neutral.
Reason (R): The number of protons equals the number of electrons in an atom.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: An atom of boron has atomic number 5 and mass number 11. Find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons.
items.markingKey: Protons = electrons = Z = 5; neutrons = A − Z = 11 − 5 = 6.

items.stem: An atom of chlorine has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. Find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons.
items.markingKey: Protons = electrons = Z = 17; neutrons = A − Z = 35 − 17 = 18.

items.stem: If the mass of a proton is taken as 1 u, estimate the mass of an atom with 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 11 electrons, and explain why the electrons are ignored.
items.answer: About 23 u (11 + 12); electrons are about 1/2000 u each, so 11 electrons add only about 0.006 u.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: 23 u. 1 mark: electron mass negligible.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "A sub-atomic particle with no charge and a mass nearly equal to that of a proton."
items.markingKey: (c) A neutron is a sub-atomic particle with no charge and a mass nearly equal to that of a proton.

items.stem: An atom of silicon has atomic number 14 and mass number 28. Find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons.
items.markingKey: Protons = electrons = Z = 14; neutrons = A − Z = 28 − 14 = 14.

items.stem: Which particles are found in the nucleus?
items.markingKey: (a) Protons and neutrons.

items.stem: An atom of neon has atomic number 10 and mass number 20. Find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons.
items.markingKey: Protons = electrons = Z = 10; neutrons = A − Z = 20 − 10 = 10.

items.stem: Why was the neutron discovered last?
items.answer: It has no charge, so it is not deflected by electric or magnetic fields and is hard to detect.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: no charge. 1 mark: hard to detect.

items.stem: Define Thomson's model of the atom.
items.answer: The model in which an atom is a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it, like seeds in a watermelon
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Thomson's model of the atom – the model in which an atom is a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it, like seeds in a watermelon.

items.stem: In Rutherford's α-particle scattering experiment: "Some α-particles were deflected through small angles." What did he conclude from this?
items.answer: The positive charge occupies very little space.
items.markingKey: (b) Some α-particles were deflected through small angles. ⇒ The positive charge occupies very little space.
options: Most of the space inside the atom is empty.
The positive charge occupies very little space.
Electrons are embedded in a positive sphere.
All the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a very small nucleus.

items.stem: How did Bohr's model overcome the drawback of Rutherford's model?
items.answer: Bohr proposed that electrons revolve only in certain permitted orbits in which they do not radiate energy, so the atom is stable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: discrete orbits. 1 mark: no energy loss/stable.

items.stem: Compare Thomson's and Rutherford's models in terms of where the positive charge and mass are located.
items.answer: Thomson: positive charge and mass spread uniformly through the atom with electrons embedded. Rutherford: positive charge and almost all mass concentrated in a tiny nucleus; electrons revolve around it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each model.

items.stem: Draw (describe) Bohr's model of a sodium atom.
items.answer: A nucleus with 11 protons and 12 neutrons; K shell 2 electrons, L shell 8, M shell 1, in fixed circular orbits.
items.markingKey: 1 mark nucleus. 1 mark shells.

items.stem: If the α-scattering experiment were done with a foil of a metal whose atoms are much lighter, such as aluminium, how might the results change? Explain.
items.answer: Fewer α-particles would be deflected through large angles, because the aluminium nucleus has much less positive charge and mass than gold, so it repels α-particles less strongly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: fewer large deflections. 1 mark: smaller nuclear charge. 1 mark: reasoning.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Electrons in Bohr's orbits do not lose energy.
Reason (R): Electrons revolve only in permitted discrete orbits.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Why did most α-particles pass straight through the gold foil?
items.answer: Most of the atom is empty space; the tiny nucleus occupies very little volume.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: empty space. 1 mark: tiny nucleus.

items.stem: Rutherford used a gold foil because:
items.answer: gold can be beaten into a very thin foil (about 1000 atoms thick)

items.stem: In Rutherford's α-particle scattering experiment: "Very few (about 1 in 12 000) α-particles bounced back." What did he conclude from this?
items.answer: All the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a very small nucleus.
items.markingKey: (b) Very few (about 1 in 12 000) α-particles bounced back. ⇒ All the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a very small nucleus.

Electrons are embedded in a positive sphere.
The positive charge occupies very little space.

items.markingKey: (d) Rutherford's model of the atom is the model with a small, dense, positive nucleus at the centre and electrons revolving around it.

items.stem: What is meant by a shell (energy level)?
items.answer: A discrete orbit around the nucleus in which electrons revolve, named K, L, M, N
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A shell (energy level) – a discrete orbit around the nucleus in which electrons revolve, named K, L, M, N.

items.stem: The maximum number of electrons in the M shell (n = 3) is:
Write the electronic configuration of lithium (Z = 3) and find its valency.
items.markingKey: (b) Configuration 2, 1 (1 mark). Outer shell has 1 electron; it loses 1 electron to complete its octet, so valency = 1 (1 mark).

items.stem: Why is the valency of chlorine 1 and not 7?
items.answer: Chlorine (2, 8, 7) needs only one electron to complete its octet, which is easier than losing seven.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: gains 1. 1 mark: easier than losing 7.

items.stem: Write the electronic configuration of nitrogen (Z = 7) and find its valency.
items.markingKey: Configuration 2, 5 (1 mark). Outer shell has 5 electrons; it shares or gains 3 electrons to complete its octet, so valency = 3 (1 mark).
